ant-18.title: Biological and Archaeological Anthropology: Variation, Stratigraphy, and Dating
explain: How can we study a distant past with no written records, and the bodies of people who look different from one another? Of the four fields of anthropology introduced in Stage 1, biological anthropology and archaeology take on this question. The two fields handle evidence differently, but they are alike in acknowledging uncertainty and building conclusions carefully. This lesson transfers the interpretive attitude learned in cultural anthropology to these two fields.

**Biological anthropology** studies the human body, evolution, and variation. According to fossil evidence, walking on two feet appeared much earlier than a large brain. Human evolution is understood as closer to a branching bush, with several lineages existing at the same time, than to a one-line staircase. The ages of fossils are usually given as ranges, and new discoveries change the picture. This differs from the ladder picture of unilineal evolutionism.

Careful clarification of concepts is needed when dealing with human **variation**. Genetic studies report that a considerable part of human genetic difference lies among individuals within the same group, that differences between groups are smaller than that, and that variation tends to change continuously with geography. The categories that divide people into a few distinct "races" on the basis of conspicuous traits such as skin color do not match biological boundaries, and the mainstream view in the field is that they are socially constructed categories. However, the fact that society actually uses and experiences those categories must be studied separately.

The first tool for reading time in archaeology is **stratigraphy**. Soil accumulates from the bottom up, so, absent disturbance, lower layers were laid down earlier than upper layers. This is called the law of superposition. But if a pit is dug later or an animal digs a burrow, soil from above enters below and the order is scrambled. This is **disturbance**. So archaeologists carefully record layer boundaries, pit outlines, and the color and texture of the soil.

explain.alt: A cross-section of a fictional excavation pit. From top to bottom there are Layer 1, Layer 2, and Layer 3, and below them bedrock. Sample A is in Layer 1 with 50% remaining, Sample B is in Layer 2 with 25% remaining, and Sample C is in Layer 3 with 12.5% remaining. On the right, a pit marked by a dotted rectangle runs down from the top to Layer 3, and the sample D inside it is labeled 50% remaining. Below, there is a note that remaining is a value taking carbon-14 in the living organism as 100%, and a note that the dotted rectangle is soil that filled a pit dug later.

explain: The representative method of obtaining absolute dates is **radiocarbon dating**. While alive, an organism replenishes carbon-14, but when it dies the replenishment stops and the remaining carbon-14 decreases at a fixed rate. The time it takes to halve, the **half-life**, is about 5730 years. The remaining fraction is $N/N_0 = (1/2)^{t/5730}$, so a sample with 50% remaining died about 5730 years ago, 25% about 11460 years ago, and 12.5% about 17190 years ago. In the figure, 50%, 25%, and 12.5% from the upper layer down matches the order of stratigraphy, in which the upper layer is more recent. Meanwhile, Sample D inside the pit is in Layer 3 yet shows 50%, similar to the sample in Layer 1. It can be interpreted that the pit was dug during the time of the upper layer and filled with soil of that time.

This method has limits too. It can be used only on organic matter containing carbon (charcoal, bone, seeds, and so on), and samples older than about 50,000 years are hard to use because too little remains. Since the concentration of carbon-14 in the past atmosphere was not constant, calibration into actual calendar dates is needed, and the result is given not as a single value but as a range of error. If a sample was contaminated or came from a disturbed layer, the date may be only the age of the sample and not the age of the layer. Large changes such as plant cultivation (known to have appeared independently in several regions after about 10,000 years ago) were also a process over a long period, not a single "revolution," and several hypotheses compete over the cause, such as climate change, population pressure, and social competition.

examples.title: Finding Age from the Remaining Fraction
body: Conditions (fictional): Calculate with a half-life of 5730 years. A charcoal sample has only 25% of its original carbon-14 remaining.
Step 1: 25% = 1/4 = (1/2) squared, so two half-lives have passed.

Interpretation: This value is the approximate age up to the time the sample died. In practice, the error range and calibration are reported together, and whether the sample was deposited at the same time as the layer must be judged separately.

examples.title: Suspecting Disturbance
body: Conditions (fictional): Sample D in the figure came from the depth of Layer 3 yet has 50% remaining. Sample A in Layer 1 is also 50%.
Step 1: Because the fractions are the same, the two samples died at almost the same time. This does not match the time of Layer 3 (12.5%).

Step 2: If a pit outline is visible around Sample D and the soil texture is different, the interpretation that a pit dug later was filled with soil from the time of the upper layer becomes persuasive.
Interpretation: Being lower does not necessarily mean being older. One must first check the possibility of disturbance and only then interpret time by the order of the strata.

ant-19.title: Integrated Problem Solving: Reading Across Theory, Evidence, and Limits
explain: So far we have learned one by one the flow of anthropological theory, kinship and exchange, ritual and symbol, health and migration, and evidence from the body and the past. This lesson is practice in using them all at once, because in real research a single case spans several theories and kinds of evidence. Here too all societies and persons are fictional.

The basic framework for solving an integrated problem is five steps. First, make the question clear. Second, distinguish the kinds of data you have (observation, interviews, documents, artifacts) and the quality of their sources. Third, choose a theoretical framework that fits the question. Fourth, interpret the evidence against the framework and compare it with competing interpretations. Fifth, state the limits of the interpretation and the contrary evidence. This order works in any subfield.

Let us summarize tips for choosing a theoretical framework. If you are curious about the use of a custom, functionalism; if you want to find the pairs beneath the surface, structuralism; if you want to unpack the meaning of behavior, interpretive anthropology. For rules of membership and marriage, descent and exchange theory; for the movement of goods, reciprocity and redistribution. For the middle state of a ritual, liminality; for taboo and pollution, classification systems; for illness, the distinction among disease, illness, and sickness. For an object spanning several places, multi-sited research; for the distant past, stratigraphy and dating.

Let us practice with a fictional case. "Blue River Village" collects grain in a storehouse every autumn, sets aside a share for ritual, and divides the rest equally. The village's three households send marriage partners in the ring C→D→E→C. When the village's old site was excavated, two strata were found overlapping. This single case uses the calculation of redistribution, the ring of generalized exchange, and the interpretation of strata and dates.

explain.alt: A cross-section of a fictional excavation pit. From top to bottom there are Layer 1, Layer 2, and Layer 3, and below them bedrock. Sample A is in Layer 1 with 50% remaining, Sample B is in Layer 2 with 25% remaining, and Sample C is in Layer 3 with 12.5% remaining. On the right, a pit marked by a dotted rectangle runs down from the top to Layer 3, and the sample D inside it is labeled 50% remaining. Below, there is a note that remaining is a value taking carbon-14 in the living organism as 100%, and a note that the dotted rectangle is soil that filled a pit dug later.

explain: Here is practice in interpreting dates. In the figure, Sample A is 50% and Sample B is 25%, so the difference in age between the two samples is 5730 years. If the difference between samples from the upper and lower layers is this large, it means that more than 5000 years passed between the two layers. However, whether the accumulation of the two layers was continuous or paused in between is judged separately from the stratigraphic record.

Finally, let us check critical reading. For any interpretation, ask yourself, "What would weaken this claim?" Check whether the evidence is only one case, whether the researcher's position biased the interpretation, and whether a competing explanation can also account for the same evidence. Writing down limits is not a confession of weakness but work that tells the reliability of the conclusion.

examples.title: Reading Redistribution and Generalized Exchange Together
body: Conditions (fictional): Six households of Blue River Village contribute 12, 8, 6, 14, 10, and 4 sacks of grain. 10% is set aside as the ritual share, and the six households divide the rest equally. And three households send marriage partners in the order C→D→E→C.

Step 1 (calculation): The total is 54 sacks, the ritual share is 5.4, the amount to divide is 48.6, and the amount received per household is 8.1 sacks. The household that contributed 14 has a net movement of −5.9.
Step 2 (structure): Redistribution reduces differences among households, and the ring of marriage maintains trust among the households. The two institutions together bind the village.

Interpretation: It can be interpreted that redistribution (goods) and generalized exchange (people) achieve the same goal, maintaining relationships, at different levels. However, this is a hypothesis, and further investigation is needed to confirm the relation between the two.

examples.title: Comparing Interpretations
body: Conditions (fictional): In a ritual of Blue River Village, people wear the same clothes for three days and do not call anyone by name. One researcher interprets it as "disorder with no order," and another as "a threshold state in which hierarchy is stripped away and a new position is received."

Step 1: Check the evidence on whether the three days of behavior follow a fixed order and whether names and positions are newly assigned after it ends. The order is fixed, and after it ends new names are received.
Step 2: The second interpretation explains both pieces of evidence, and the first does not.
Interpretation: The second interpretation is more persuasive. But leave it open to revision if new evidence appears, and state also what evidence would weaken the interpretation.

ant-20.title: Undergraduate Capstone: Integrated Analysis of the Fictional Blue River Village Data
explain: This capstone is the final assignment of the whole department. You read the field data and excavation data collected in the fictional "Blue River Village" (Pureungang) and bind theoretical frameworks, evidence, and limits into a single interpretation. It is not a problem with one fixed correct answer but an assignment to write an explanation backed by grounds. All the data are fictional and have no relation to any real group.

Data 1 (field notes). This is a grain-sharing ritual held at the village storehouse after the autumn harvest. Six households contribute 10, 6, 14, 8, 12, and 10 sacks of grain. A ritual share of 20% is set aside, and the six households divide the rest equally. On the day before the ritual, people speak little and wear the same white clothes. The villagers say, "A household that gives a lot is treated as an elder for a year."

Data 2 (kinship and marriage). The village has three households, C, D, and E. When marrying, people of household C go to D, people of D go to E, and people of E go to C. Descent is patrilineal, and people do not marry someone of the same line. An old man said, "Household C is very worried because household D could not send anyone this year."

Data 3 (excavation). The old site of the village was excavated, and Layer 1 (top), Layer 2, and Layer 3 were obtained. The carbon-14 remaining in charcoal samples was 50% in Layer 1, 25% in Layer 2, and 12.5% in Layer 3. A sample inside a pit at the depth of Layer 3 was 50%, and a pit outline was visible around it. In Layer 2, traces of a grain-storage pit were found.

We propose a framework for the analysis. (1) Use a redistribution calculation to find each household's gain or loss, and read the reward to the household that gives a lot through interpretation of meaning (thick description). (2) Analyze the ring of marriage as generalized exchange, and explain the consequences when one household cannot send anyone. (3) Examine whether wearing the same clothes and speaking little is the liminal state of the ritual. (4) Read stratigraphy, dates, and disturbance in the excavation data. (5) State the limits of each interpretation and the competing explanations.

There are points to observe when writing. Write the evidence first and the interpretation afterward. Do not assert, and write in the form "it can be interpreted as...". Do not try to explain everything with one theory, and write what the theory explains well and what it misses. This assignment is not guidance for real fieldwork or excavation, and it is not fact about any group.

examples.title: A Weak Interpretation and a Strong Interpretation
body: Conditions: Interpret the white clothes and speaking little in Data 1.
Step 1 (weak interpretation): "The villagers regard the ritual as important." This is a generality that is not connected to any part of the data.

Step 2 (strong interpretation): "The behavior of wearing the same white clothes and speaking little on the day before the ritual has a liminal character that reduces the usual hierarchy, and the fact that the household that gave a lot is treated as an elder the year after the ritual can be read as a new hierarchy arising in the incorporation stage. However, since the meaning of the white clothes was not confirmed directly with the villagers, this is a hypothesis."
Interpretation: A strong interpretation points to the evidence, connects the theory, and states the limits.

examples.title: Reading the Excavation Data
body: Conditions: Interpret the sample inside the pit in Data 3 (50%) and the sample in Layer 3 (12.5%).
Step 1: The sample inside the pit has a date similar to Layer 1, so it differs from the date of Layer 3. Since a pit outline exists, the evidence of disturbance overlaps.

Step 2: Obtain the time of Layer 3 from the 12.5% sample, and estimate the traces of the grain-storage pit found in Layer 2 as activity from the time of the 25% sample, that is, about 11460 years ago.

Interpretation: One cannot conclude straight away from traces of grain storage that the village had a redistribution institution. There is a gap of interpretation between the fact of storage and an institution of distribution.

checks.prompt: In Data 1, six households contribute 10, 6, 14, 8, 12, and 10 sacks, 20% is set aside as the ritual share, and the rest is divided equally. How many sacks is the net movement (amount received − amount contributed) of the household that contributed 14 sacks? (unit: sacks)
checks.hint: Find the total, subtract 20%, then divide by 6.
checks.explanation: The total is 60, the ritual share is 12, the amount to divide is 48, and each household gets 8 sacks. 8 − 14 = −6.

checks.prompt: In Data 2, household D could not send anyone this year. By the logic of generalized exchange, what is the most directly expected result?
checks.hint: In the direction C→D→E→C, see where the arrow leaving D goes.
checks.explanation: If D cannot send anyone, E, which receives people from D, is affected, and the balance of the whole ring is shaken. The data in which the old man worried about household C can be read as anxiety of the whole ring.
options: Household E loses those it was to receive, and the balance of the ring is shaken
Household E sending to household C is not affected at all
The ring automatically changes into restricted exchange
All households change to endogamy

checks.prompt: Choose one of Data 1-3, and in 3-4 sentences write one interpretation that connects the evidence with a theoretical framework. State one limit as well.
checks.hint: Write in the order of evidence, theory, and limit.
checks.explanation: Connecting evidence and theory, and stating the limit, are the requirements of a good interpretation.
checks.model: In Data 1, the behavior of wearing the same white clothes and speaking little on the day before the ritual is evidence that can be interpreted, in the framework of liminality, as a stage in which the usual hierarchy is reduced. That the household that gave a lot is treated as an elder after the ritual can be read as a new hierarchy arising in the incorporation stage. However, since the meaning of the white clothes was not confirmed directly with the villagers, this interpretation is a hypothesis and a limit, and it must be confirmed through additional interviews.
